content: The nasal helm was a type of helmet that gained widespread use from the late Dark Ages through the Early Medieval period. It featured a domed or raised center, typically constructed around a basic skull-cap design. A distinctive characteristic of this helm was a single protruding strip of metal that extended down over the nose, providing additional protection to the face. This design first appeared in Europe during the late 9th century and quickly became the dominant form of head protection, replacing earlier designs such as the pudding-bowl helm and the spectacle helm. One of the earliest known examples of this type of helmet is the Vasgaard Helm. The Bayeux Tapestry, a famous historical artifact, depicts numerous examples of nasal helms, highlighting their popularity during that era. By the 13th century, nasal helms began to be phased out in favor of helmets that offered more comprehensive facial protection. Despite this decline in use among higher-ranking knights and men-at-arms, nasal helms continued to be utilized by archers, for whom an unobstructed field of vision was essential. Nasal helms were constructed using two primary methods: some were made as a single piece, while others were of spangenhelm construction, which involved multiple metal segments joined together. In later periods, nasal helms were often crafted with a single, smooth, raised dome to allow weapons to deflect more easily upon impact.
